reaction-representations-s1.title: Carbon monoxide burning
reaction-representations-s1.html: Key: dark circle labeled C, carbon atom; red circle labeled O, oxygen atom. All species are gases.

reaction-representations-s2.title: Two elements combine
reaction-representations-s2.html: Key: blue circle X, an atom of element X; orange circle Y, an atom of element Y. Every species is a gas.

items.q: Which balanced equation is shown by the diagram?
options: 2CO(g) + O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g)
4CO(g) + 3O₂(g) → 4CO₂(g) + O₂(g)
CO(g) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g)
CO(g) + O(g) → CO₂(g)

why.correct: Two O₂ molecules were used (3 before, 1 after) to turn 4 CO into 4 CO₂, a 4 : 2 : 4 ratio, which is 2 : 1 : 2. The leftover O₂ did not react, so it is not part of the equation.
options: Right: the ratio of what reacted, in smallest whole numbers.
Puts the unreacted O₂ on both sides. An equation shows what reacts in what ratio, not the leftover amount in one particular mixture.
Unbalanced: 3 O atoms on the left and 2 on the right.
Oxygen gas exists as O₂ molecules, as the diagram shows, not as single O atoms.

items.q: Which reactant is in excess in this mixture?
options: O₂, because one O₂ molecule is left after all the CO has reacted
CO, because there are more CO molecules than O₂ molecules to start
CO₂, because it is the most plentiful species after the reaction
Neither, since each atom in the Before box is also in the After box

why.correct: The reactant left over is the one in excess. All four CO molecules were used; one O₂ remains.
options: Right: some O₂ is left unreacted.
Starting with more particles does not make a reactant the excess one; what matters is the ratio needed. Each O₂ handles two CO, so 3 O₂ could handle 6 CO.
CO₂ is a product, not a reactant.
Atoms are always conserved, but that does not mean both reactants were used up.

items.q: How many more CO molecules would need to be added to the Before box so that both reactants are used up completely?

mistakes.why: Value: one O₂ is left, and each O₂ reacts with two CO (2CO + O₂). It needs two more CO molecules.
Value: that is the total CO needed for 3 O₂, not the number to add. Four are already there.

why.correct: Three O₂ need 3 × 2 = 6 CO. The box has 4, so add 2 more. Equivalently, the one leftover O₂ needs 2 CO.

items.q: If this reaction were carried out in a sealed, rigid container, how would the total number of gas molecules change, and why?
options: It falls from 7 to 5, since 3 reactant molecules make 2 product ones
It stays at 7, since atoms are conserved in a reaction
It increases, because CO₂ molecules are larger than CO molecules
It decreases, because some atoms combine into the solid walls

why.correct: Count: 4 CO + 3 O₂ = 7 molecules before; 4 CO₂ + 1 O₂ = 5 after. The equation 2CO + O₂ → 2CO₂ turns 3 gas molecules into 2.
options: Right: 7 molecules become 5.
Atoms are conserved, but molecules are not; atoms regroup into fewer, larger molecules.
The number of molecules, not their size, is what is counted, and that number goes down.
All atoms stay in gas molecules, as the After box shows; none leave the gas.

items.q: Which equation describes the reaction in the diagram?
options: X₂(g) + 3Y₂(g) → 2XY₃(g)
3X₂(g) + 6Y₂(g) → 4XY₃(g) + X₂(g)
X(g) + 3Y(g) → XY₃(g)
2X₂(g) + 6Y₂(g) → 4XY₃(g)

why.correct: Used: 2 X₂ (3 before, 1 after) and 6 Y₂, making 4 XY₃. The ratio 2 : 6 : 4 reduces to 1 : 3 : 2.
options: Right: the reacting ratio in smallest whole numbers.
Includes the leftover X₂ on both sides; leave unreacted particles out of the equation.
The elements are drawn as two-atom molecules, X₂ and Y₂.
Balanced, and the right ratio, but every coefficient can be halved.

items.q: Which reactant limits the amount of XY₃ that forms?
options: Y₂, because all six Y₂ molecules are used up
X₂, because there are fewer X₂ molecules than Y₂ molecules
X₂, because one X₂ molecule is left over
Neither, because the box contains equal numbers of X and Y atoms

why.correct: The limiting reactant is the one that runs out. No Y₂ remains, while one X₂ does; Y₂ ran out first.
options: Right: Y₂ is used up, so it sets how much product forms.
Fewer particles does not mean limiting; each X₂ needs three Y₂, so X₂ goes further.
A leftover reactant is the one in excess, the opposite of limiting.
There are 6 X atoms and 12 Y atoms, which are not equal; in any case the ratio needed (1 : 3), not equality, decides.

items.q: A new box starts with 5 X₂ and 9 Y₂ molecules. How many XY₃ molecules can form?

mistakes.why: Value: that is how many XY₃ the X₂ could make if Y₂ were plentiful. 9 Y₂ is not enough for 5 X₂ (that needs 15 Y₂), so Y₂ limits.
Value: 9 Y₂ react with 3 X₂, but each X₂ gives two XY₃. Use the 3 : 2 ratio of Y₂ to XY₃.

why.correct: For 5 X₂ you would need 15 Y₂; there are only 9, so Y₂ limits. 9 Y₂ × (2 XY₃ / 3 Y₂) = 6 XY₃. Check atoms: 6 XY₃ hold 6 X and 18 Y; 3 X₂ are used and 2 X₂ are left.

items.q: Which feature of a correct reaction particle diagram does the After box show?
options: The same number of each kind of atom as the Before box
The same number of molecules as the Before box
One product particle for each reactant particle
Equal numbers of reactant and product molecules

why.correct: There are 6 X and 12 Y atoms in each box. The molecules regroup (9 before, 5 after), so molecule counts need not match; atom counts must.
options: Right: atoms are conserved, so each kind of atom is counted the same in both boxes.
There are 9 molecules before and 5 after; molecules are not conserved.
Particles do not pair off one-to-one; here 1 X₂ and 3 Y₂ make 2 XY₃, as the coefficients say.
The coefficients, not a rule of equality, set how many of each appear.

items.q: Table salt is heated above its melting point, 801 °C, until it is completely melted. Which formula with a state symbol describes it?
options: NaCl(l)
NaCl(aq)
NaCl(s)
NaCl(g)

why.correct: Melted salt is a pure liquid, so (l). (aq) would mean dissolved in water, and there is no water here.
options: Right: a melted pure substance is a liquid.
(aq) means dissolved in water; melted salt contains no water.
(s) is the salt before it melts.
Salt does not boil until far above its melting point; at this stage it is a liquid.

items.q: In the equation 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l), what does changing (l) to (g) for water describe?
options: The same reaction, with the water formed as vapor rather than liquid
A different reaction that uses different reactants
A reaction that forms more molecules of water
Nothing; state symbols are just labels and change no meaning

why.correct: The state symbol tells how the product exists. The atoms and coefficients are unchanged; the water is gas instead of liquid, which matters later for energy.
options: Right: same atoms and ratio; water as vapor.
The reactants are unchanged; only the state of the product differs.
The coefficients, not the state symbol, set how many molecules form.
State symbols carry meaning: liquid water and water vapor are different states of the same substance.

items.q: A student draws a particle diagram for 2Na(s) + Cl₂(g) → 2NaCl(s). Which drawing of the product is best?
options: A packed, alternating array of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions
Separate NaCl molecules spread through the box
Na atoms and Cl atoms mixed at random, not touching
Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions spread apart, each surrounded by water

why.correct: NaCl(s) is an ionic solid: a lattice of alternating cations and anions packed close together. There are no separate molecules.
options: Right: an ionic solid is an extended array of alternating ions.
Ionic compounds do not form discrete molecules; the formula NaCl is a ratio of ions.
In the product the elements are ions held together, not separate neutral atoms.
That shows NaCl(aq); the equation says (s) and there is no water.

items.q: A box holds 6 N₂ and 12 H₂ molecules. They react by N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ until one reactant is used up. How many reactant molecules are left over?

mistakes.why: Value: you used 4 N₂ instead of counting what is left. 12 H₂ react with 4 N₂, so 6 − 4 = 2 N₂ remain.
Value: 8 is the number of NH₃ formed, not the leftover reactant.

why.correct: 12 H₂ need 12 ÷ 3 = 4 N₂. There are 6 N₂, so H₂ runs out first and 6 − 4 = 2 N₂ molecules are left. 8 NH₃ form.

items.q: A student draws the reaction 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2SO₃(g). Before: 4 SO₂ and 2 O₂. After: 4 SO₃ and 1 O₂. Which errors does the drawing contain? Select all that apply.
options: It has more oxygen atoms after than before
The After box should hold no O₂ at all, since the starting amounts match the 2 : 1 ratio
It shows the wrong number of SO₃ molecules
It shows sulfur atoms being created

why.correct: 4 SO₂ + 2 O₂ = 4 S and 12 O before. 4 SO₃ + 1 O₂ = 4 S and 14 O after: two oxygen atoms appeared. 4 SO₂ and 2 O₂ are in the exact 2 : 1 ratio, so both should be used up, giving 4 SO₃ and nothing else.
options: Right: 12 O atoms before, 14 after.
Right: the reactants are in the exact ratio, so no O₂ should remain.
4 SO₂ make 4 SO₃, which is the right number.
There are 4 S atoms in each box.

items.q: A diagram shows 6 molecules of AB₂ before a reaction and, after it, 6 molecules of AB plus 3 molecules of B₂. Which equation fits?
options: 2AB₂ → 2AB + B₂
AB₂ → AB + B
6AB₂ → 6AB + 3B₂ + AB₂
AB₂ → A + B₂

why.correct: Ratio 6 : 6 : 3 reduces to 2 : 2 : 1. Check: 2 A and 4 B on each side.
options: Right: the counts reduce to 2 : 2 : 1 and atoms balance.
The diagram shows B leaving as B₂ molecules, not single atoms.
Adds a molecule that is not in the diagram and keeps the large counts.
The diagram shows AB molecules, not separate A atoms, as a product.

items.q: A sealed box holds 3 CH₄ and 4 O₂ molecules. They react by CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g) until one reactant runs out. Which list gives the contents of the box afterward?
options: 1 CH₄, 2 CO₂ and 4 H₂O
3 CO₂ and 6 H₂O
2 CO₂, 4 H₂O and 1 O₂
1 CH₄, 2 CO₂ and 2 H₂O

why.correct: Three CH₄ would need 6 O₂; there are only 4, so O₂ is limiting. 4 O₂ react with 2 CH₄ and make 2 CO₂ and 4 H₂O; 1 CH₄ is left. Atom check: 3 C, 12 H and 8 O in both lists.
options: Right: O₂ runs out, leaving one CH₄; atoms balance.
Uses all the CH₄ as if O₂ were plentiful; that would need 6 O₂ and creates oxygen atoms.
Treats CH₄ as limiting, but 4 O₂ are not enough for 3 CH₄; this list also has too few carbon atoms.
Forgets the coefficient 2 on water: each CH₄ gives two H₂O, so hydrogen atoms go missing.
